To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the incidence of breast cancer in Western Australia was estimated to be 100.2 per 100 000 in 1989 (95% confidence interval 97.0 to 103.5).

the lifetime risk of breast tumour development in Western Australian women is 10%, that 68% of tumours are first detected by the women herself, and that mammographic screening plays only a small role at present in the detection of tumours.

the estimated lifetime risk of breast tumour is higher than previously thought, that the majority of tumours occur in women who will have access to mammography, and that mammography will detect more tumours at an early stage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epidemiology of breast cancer and the role of screening in the early detection of breast cancer.
(1) the incidence and distribution of breast cancer, (2) the detection of breast cancers, (3) the treatment and management of breast cancers, and (4) the outcome of breast cancer treatment in WA.
the following questions: 1. What proportion of cases are not known to the Cancer Registry? 2. What proportion of tumours is detected by mammographic breast cancer screening?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
breast cancer in WA is a significant public health problem.

breast cancer in Western Australia (1989) was a disease of middle aged women, most commonly presenting with a lump, and that the tumour was most likely to be a small, well-differentiated, node-negative invasive carcinoma.
the incidence of breast cancer in Western Australia has not been previously estimated and that the present study is the first attempt to provide this information.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
1. The State Cancer Registry is not capturing all breast cancers diagnosed in Western Australia.
breast cancer is a common and serious disease in WA.

the risk is 10%, that 68% of tumours are first detected by the women themselves, that 11% are found by doctors and only 11% by mammographic screening, that 40% of cases present with Stage I disease and 39% with Stage II disease, and that 84% of women are in an age range that would allow them access to mammographic breast screening.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mammography screening is not the only answer.

we have shown that the incidence of breast cancer in Western Australia (the state of Western Australia) is much higher than previously thought, and it’s much higher than the average for the rest of the world.
mammographic screening is a good idea, and that it will be more effective if it is started at age 40.
